doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Asking for space and recording with Ben Riley
summary: He asks sidemen for space but never how to play; recounts the Sharp Nine date with Ben Riley, Hazeltine and Washington.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Do you, as a singer, you’re usually the featured performer. Is that a fair statement?
So do you feel that you have the license to ask a person to play differently?

It depends. If I hire musicians for a date then I’m hiring them to play what they play. I’m hiring them to play them. If I’m working with a trio and I don’t know the trio, or even if I do, if I want less from somebody, or if I want more space, I don’t have a problem in asking them for more space. And that’s what I’ll do. I’ll ask them. Could you give me more space.
That’s the word you would use.
But I’m not going to tell anybody how to play. I might ask for someone to play softer, but I’ll never say, “hey could you play more like Freddie Green?” I don’t think that’s right.
“Could you play more like Ben Riley?” “Well why don’t you call Ben Riley if you wanted that?” I mean I had the good fortune to record with Ben Riley.

And there were several Monk tunes on the record that the record company cat, Marc Edelman from Sharp Nine Records. It was David Hazeltine on piano, Peter Washington, Jim Rotundi on trumpet, and Ben Riley. I show up and I see Ben Riley and I went wow. We’re doing “Epistrophy” with my lyrics, “Ask Me Now,” “Speed Ball,” a couple of tunes like that. And Ben Riley is looking at the list of songs. And he says to me, “you a tenor player?” I said, “no, I’m a singer.” Can I use French on this?

He said to me, “a singer? You going to sing this shit?” I said, “yes, sir.” He said, “my man.” So that, I mean there you go. I mean Ben Riley, I got all the respect in the world for Ben Riley. But he was happy that I was singing “Speed Ball” and “Night in Tunisia” because I’m singing a real, what I like to think of as a real jazz repertoire.
